en: Itivuttaka 56: Tikanipāta, Paṭhamavagga Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard: “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a stone, the person who is like a water jar, and the person who is like a rain cloud. And how, monks, is a person like a stone? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hate, harboring ill will toward beings. Just as a stone, when struck, does not feel pain, does not experience aversion, and does not give rise to an angry thought; even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of hate, harboring ill will toward beings. This, monks, is called a person like a stone. And how, monks, is a person like a water jar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of lust, desiring sensual pleasures. Just as a water jar, when struck, feels pain, experiences aversion, and gives rise to an angry thought; even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of lust, desiring sensual pleasures. This, monks, is called a person like a water jar. And how, monks, is a person like a rain cloud? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from lust, without desire for sensual pleasures. Just as a rain cloud, when struck, does not feel pain, does not experience aversion, and does not give rise to an angry thought; even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind free from lust, without desire for sensual pleasures. This, monks, is called a person like a rain cloud. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, friends! “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the venerable Ānanda. The venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, it was said by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world… [as above]… These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Now, friends, what is the meaning of this statement? “Friend Ānanda, we do not know the meaning of this statement spoken by the Blessed One. It would be good, friend Ānanda, if you could explain the meaning of this statement spoken by the Blessed One. “Then listen, friends, and pay close attention. I shall speak. “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the venerable Ānanda. The venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, that person who is like a stone is one who has abandoned the lower fetters and is bound by the upper fetters. That person who is like a water jar is one who has abandoned the lower fetters and is bound by the upper fetters. That person who is like a rain cloud is one who is an arahant, with outflows exhausted. This, friends, is the meaning of the statement spoken by the Blessed One. When this was said, the venerable Sāriputta said to the venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, it is well said! Friend Ānanda, it is well said! For if the meaning of this statement spoken by the Blessed One were not explained by the venerable Ānanda, it would have remained unexplained; but since it has been explained by the venerable Ānanda, it is now clearly understood. It is just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. Even so, friend Ānanda, the Dhamma has been made clear by the venerable Ānanda in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the venerable Ānanda accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”
The First Discourse on the Taints.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:
The taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance—
these, monks, are the three taints.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
The disciple of the mindful Buddha understands the taints and the origin of the taints.
and the path leading to their destruction—
through the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu [is liberated].
“Free from hunger, he has attained final Nibbāna.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
